4. The pre-emption case was allowed by the Munsif, Jamalpur, and on appeal by the appellants, the judgment was reversed by the Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Mymensingh. The learned Subordinate Judge held that the pre-emption case was not maintainable in the absence of some of the co-sharers by Inheritance. On a revisional application filed by the pre-emptor-respondent under section 113 of the Code of Civil Procedure the learned Single Judge of the High Court of Bangladesh set aside the judgment of the lower Appellate Court holding that the pre-emption case should not be dismissed on the ground of non-joinder of necessary parties. It is not necessary that all the co-sharers of the holding should be impleaded in the pre-emption proceeding. In taking this view the learned Judge referred to the decision In Motilal Sikder vs. Benodini Dasi. The learned Judge held that the provision of sub-section (2) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 regarding parties to the proceeding is directory, and not mandatory; and, as such, the pre-emption application was not bad for defect of parties. On this view the judgment of lower Appellate Court was set aside. 

 "It does not appear from a perusal of the provisions of section 96 that it was the intent of the legislature that the penalty for non-impleading a person as contemplated in sub-section (2) Is the invalidity of the order which may ultimately be made in the said proceeding. The question whether a person re a necessary party under sub-section (2) is a question of fact and the object of this provision seems to provide the co-sharer tenants and the holders to the contiguous lands with the opportunity of availing of the provision of the said sub-section. Since the benefit conferred under the said provision is meant for certain individuals, they can very well of waived. In that view of the matter the positive injunction contained in the said sub section as to the making of parties in spite of its being couched in mandatory language, should be read as directory". 

 11. While considering the ground upon which the leave was granted his Lordship observed that the question of joinder of partner is essentially a matter of procedure and some detailed rules have been provided in the Code of Civil Procedure. On the question of joinder of parties, in the course of discussion of this question, his Lordship observed that Order I of the Code of Civil Procedure deals with the question of the parties to a suit and by virtue of section 141 of the Code, the said provisions are applicable to a proceeding of original nature like the one under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The discussion, however, mainly centred on the rules of pleading which provide that any objection as to the maintainability of a suit which requires investigation of acts must be taken in the pleading before the framing of the issues. So that the other party may not be taken by surprise and is prejudiced in the matter of taking steps to meet the objection. According to his Lordship the principle relating to a partition suit has got no application to a proceeding for pre-emption His Lords ship referred to a decision of a Single Judge of the High Court in the care of Syed Abdul Karim vs. Harendre Cnandra Dhupi, 14 DLR 847 which contains the following observation: 

 13. The above quotations provide sufficient indication as to the manner how the appeal under consideration was disposed of. The petitioners were allowed to take an additional ground showing defect of party at the hearing of the rule which was not taken at the trial of the pre-emption case and objection on the ground of non-joinder of necessary parties was not pressed at the trial. The pre-emption application was dismissed only on accepting the objection which was taken for the first time in revision and without sending the case back to the trial Court to find out as to whether the said persons omitted from the proceeding had any subsisting interest in the land as shown by the pre-emptee. The uncontroverted statement of the appellants made in respect of the subsisting interest of Mozaffar Ali Khan was accepted. It was stated that there was a subsequent partition of the lands purchased by Exhibit 1 (b) between the two brothers and the portion which fell in the share of Ledu Khan was contiguous to the land under pre-emption and the portion which was allotted to Mozaffar Ali Khan was not contiguous to the said lands. In this background the appeal was allowed and judgment of the High Court was set aside and the judgment of the Courts below were restored. 

 16. The right to purchase the land transferred as contemplated under section 96 is a statutory right and it is to be exercised within 4 months of the service of notice under section 89, or if no notice has been served under section 89, within four months of the date of knowledge of the transfer. The right to purchase the land has been very clearly and unambiguously spelt out by the legislature in the section. The language of the provisions in different parts of the section shows that the right to purchase conferred upon the co-sharer tenants or the contiguous land owners is not by any means dependent upon initiation of the pre-emption proceeding either by a co-sharer tenant or owner of the land contiguous to the land of transfer. However, the section does not cast any duty upon the Court to find out through process of enquiry all the non-notified co-sharers if any or all the non-impleaded contiguous land owners, and for complete adjudication implead them In the proceedings, Sub-section (2) requires that all the co-sharer tenants of the holding are to be impleaded in the application failing under the first part of sub-section (1). Similarly, all the contiguous land owners are to be made parties in the application failing under the second part of sub-section (1), Sab-section (4) provides the period of limitation for the remaining co-sharer tenant or the tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred, to join in the pre-emption proceedings. This period of two months begins to run from the service of notice of the application for pre-emption. The different provisions of section 96 clearly point out that a duty has been cast upon the pre-emptor, if he is a co-sharer tenant, to make all the remaining co-sharer tenants, and if he is a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred, all the remaining tenants boiling lands contiguous to the land transferred and the transferee, parties to the application. Object of sub-section (2) is to have all the co-sharer tenants or all the tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred, before the Court for proper and complete adjudication in accordance with law. A co-sharer tenant or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred may waive his right to purchase the land, but on this consideration there is hardly any scope for taking the view that the requirement of sub-section (2) is not mandatory but is me rely directory. Second Part of sub-section (4) clearly indicates that a co-sharer tenant or a tenant having land contiguous to the land transferred failing to join in the pre-emption proceeding within the given time, shall not have any further right to purchase under this section. Waive of the right is one thing, but defeating the right by deliberate omission in the pre-emption application is a different thing. There is hardly any scope to doubt that the clear object, of legislation is that all the parties having right of pre-emption should be before the Court for adjudication of the right or rights of pre-emption in accordance with law. 

 18. The procedure with regard to misjoinder and non-joinder of parties in a suit or a proceeding in any Court of civil jurisdiction, in view of section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure, Order 1. rule 9 is applicable. Order 1, rule 9 reads as under:— 

 "No suit shall be defeated by reason of the misjoinder or non-joinder of parties, and the Court may in every suit deal with the matter in controversy so far as regards the rights and interest of the parties actually before it." 

 19. The question of non-joinder of necessary party affecting framing of a pre-emption application is to be decided keeping in view the requirement of the different sub-sections of section 96 along with the provisions as contained in Order 1, rules 9 and 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, because, Pre-emption proceedings being one of the proceedings as contemplated under section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure the procedure of law in Order I, rule 9 is applicable. On account of omission of necessary party a preemption case shall not be dismissed outright keeping In view the provision of Order 1, role 9, inasmuch as non-joinder of necessary party will not by itself defeat a suit proceeding However, the special statutory provision in sub-section (2) as to the necessary parties to be impleaded is mandatory. In clear language it mentions the persons to be impleaded in an application made under sub-section (1) by a co-sharer tenant: and in an application made by a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred. Requirement of the statutory provision cannot be minimised by the procedural law as contained in Order 1, rule 9. The special provision in sub section (2) is not controlled by Order 1, rule 9, which merely provides that a suit shall not be dismissed by reason of mere non-joinder of necessary parties. Order 1, rule 10 provides for addition of party at any stage of the proceedings, either upon or without the application of either party. Where there is non-joinder of a necessary party the Court is ems powered to add the necessary party under rule 10 at any stage of the proceeding, either upon or without the application of either party. The objection as to non-joinder of necessary parties must be taken at the earliest opportunity by the defendant. Such objection provides an opportunity to the plains tiff to remove the defect by adding parties who were omitted. In taking objection on the ground of non-joinder of necessary parties the defendant is required to furnish the names and particulars of the parties who were omitted from the suit. On the refusal of the plaintiff to implead the parties mentioned in the written statement, the question becomes an issue for adjudication by the Court and on adjudication the question becomes decided. In such an event the consequences must follow, that is, the suit becomes liable to be dismissed on the ground of non-joinder of necessary party. In the case of a pre-emption preceding the law regarding procedure cannot be treated as different. If the pre-emptee or for that matter any of the parties disclose existence of a necessary party and furnishes the necessary particulars, but the pre-emptor still insists not to implead him as a party, consequence on adjudication is the same. It has already been mentioned that such objection regarding non-joinder of necessary parties should be taken at the earlier opportunity, before the trial, because an enquiry on this question may be necessary. Of course, in an appropriate case such objection may be allowed to be raised in the appeal. This may be done on the ground that the appeal is continuation of the suit or proceeding. But there is no scope for raising the question of defect of party on account of non-joinder of necessary parties, for the first time in revision. 

 24. The provision of law as contained to sub-section (2) should be followed without minimising its requirement. The requirement as to making of parties is undoubtedly positive. It is the duty of the pre-emptor to implead the necessary parties as I have already observed above that this requirement of law should be enforced keeping in view the provisions of Order 1, rules 9 and 10 if the prey emptor, after getting an opportunity, fails to amend his application by impleading the necessary parties as pointed out by the pre-emptee, and on evidence if it is found that the application suffers from defect of parties, in that event the application cannot succeed and must be dismissed. I fully agree with the view expressed in the case reported in 14 DLR 847 that presence of the persons mentioned in sub-section (2) of section 96 " is not only a matter of convenience but of absolute necessity to enable the Court to adjudicate more effectively and completely". Otherwise, a non-notified co-sharer or a contiguous land owner may have an occasion to challenge the decision and to try to re-open the matter. The decision in Motilal Sikder vs. Benodini Dasi, should be read in the light of the observations made above. 

 25. The learned Single Judge while upsetting the decision of the lower Appellate Court omitted to notice that the pre-emption case was dismissed mainly on the ground that the pre-emptors failed to implead the necessary parties in spite of opportunity given to them by supplying the names in the written objection; and that on evidence it was found by the lower Appellate Court that the persons named in the written objection were co-sharers by inheritance having subsisting Interest in the holding, and In their absence the pre-emption case was not maintainable. The learned Judge in considering the question whether the sub-section (2) is directory or mandatory observed that non-inclusion of the persons named by the pre-emptees does not affect the application for pre-emption. "since the benefit of pre-emption is an individual opportunity and, as such, may be waived". Right to purchase a land may be waived, but that cannot be made a ground to relax the mandate of the statute to implead the necessary parties in the proceeding. A co-sharer in the holding cannot be allowed to purchase the entire land without impleading the other co-sharers and thereby depriving them from getting their share Similarly, a tenant owning land contiguous to the land transferred cannot be allowed to purchase the entire land transferred without impleading the other tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred, and thereby depriving them from exercising their right in the case of second category of pre-emptors presence of other tenants or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred is necessary for the purpose of determination of the order of priority as among the tenants in the manner as indicated in clause (b) of sub-section (5). So, presence of all the persons mentioned in sub-section (2), as the case may be, is more a matter of absolute necessity than of mere convenience. Their presence is necessary, so that the Court can adjudicate the claim of pre-emption more effectively and completely.
